summary:
Chechnya is a republic within the Russian Federation and stands under the national framework, including the national restrictions on legal gender recognition and public expression that the national record carries. Within that framework, the exposure a trans visitor faces in Chechnya is materially harsher than the national baseline, because the republic's own authorities are the documented source of the violence rather than a protection against it.

Chechen authorities apply religious law in matters of sexuality, in conflict with Russian federal law and with the Chechen constitution's own provision that the republic is secular and that no religion may be made official or mandatory. Religious courts have imposed the death penalty for homosexuality and adultery since sharia law was introduced under president Aslan Maskhadov in 1999. Russian LGBT legislation formally applies in the republic, but no protection operates in practice, and authorities are reported to encourage families to kill relatives suspected of homosexuality.

Human Rights Watch documented the February 2017 purge: men believed to be gay were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities for days, humiliated, starved and tortured. Some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families barely alive from beatings, with captors outing them and urging honour killings. The organisation established that top regional officials knew of the operation despite Ramzan Kadyrov's denial.

The detentions began in late March 2017 and took in more than 100 men, and possibly several hundred, across Grozny and other settlements, among them muftiate religious figures and television presenters who had concealed their orientation. Detainees were held in a secret prison in Argun and in other detention centres, beaten and tortured with electric shocks; at least three were beaten to death and reports put the toll as high as 20. Human Rights Watch recorded at least three deaths. Released detainees fled the republic.

Those who stayed faced continuing risk of persecution by the authorities and of honour killings by relatives, with no safe route of complaint or judicial recourse because retaliation was practically inevitable.

Persecution resumed within two years. Novaya Gazeta reported in January 2019 that warnings were circulating through VKontakte LGBT group administrators telling those still at large to leave the republic, and that Kadyrov's press secretary Alvi Karimov denied the reports. A renewed purge beginning in December 2018 detained around 40 people, including gay men and women, with two killed; by May 2019 police had resumed unlawful detentions, beatings and humiliation of men presumed gay or bisexual. No criminal case was opened into the April 2017 investigation into torture and killings of gay men.

Since 2022 the security apparatus has used military conscription as a further instrument against detained men. The Insider reported on 4 September 2024, citing the monitoring group SK SOS, that Chechen security forces coerced detained gay men into military service, with at least seven sent to the frontlines in Ukraine and one already killed, and that the practice predated the 21 September 2022 mobilisation order. In early September 2022 six men were detained on suspicion of homosexuality, threatened with fabricated charges and warned that they would be sent to the front.

The coercion operates inside a wider conscription machinery. A Memorial Human Rights Centre investigation found a mass wave of unlawful detentions in Chechnya with detainees forcibly sent to fight in Ukraine: people were detained over minor pretexts such as missing insurance documents, taken to police departments, subjected to psychological pressure and physical abuse, and forced to sign contracts, while families sometimes had to recruit two volunteers to free a detained relative.

The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (version 2.0, June 2025) records systematic anti-LGBT campaigns in Chechnya and across the wider North Caucasus between 2017 and 2024, involving abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings, and assesses that in the North Caucasus trans people and publicly active LGBT+ advocates are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution.
tangentialFactors:
The documented violence has drawn no domestic criminal accountability. The only formal response identified is external: in March 2021 the European Union imposed sanctions on two Chechen government officials over government-sponsored violence against LGBTQIA+ individuals.

The pattern is not confined to this republic. The UK Home Office assessment covers the wider North Caucasus, so movement to neighbouring republics in the same mountain region does not remove the risk that Chechen practice creates.

The republic's enforcement of religious law sits in direct conflict with Russian federal law and with the Chechen constitution's secular clause; that conflict has not produced federal intervention to restrain regional authorities or to protect LGBT residents and visitors.
localsOnly:
Warnings were circulated through VKontakte LGBT group administrators telling those still at large to leave the republic. Users abandoned LGBT messenger groups and closed social media accounts because a non-traditional orientation carries lethal honour-based retaliation under close social monitoring, and those released from detention fled the republic.

Families are drawn into the security apparatus. Captors outed detainees to their relatives and urged honour killings; in the conscription wave, families have sometimes had to recruit two volunteers to secure the release of a detained relative.

Detention can be triggered on trivial pretexts, including missing insurance documents, which places anyone in the republic who comes to police attention at risk of being taken to a police department, abused and pressed into a military contract.
outOfScopeNotes:
The death toll of the 2017 purge is not settled. At least three killings are documented, with reporting putting the figure as high as 20; no consolidated official figure exists because the Russian state does not record hate crimes against the LGBT community, and Chechen authorities deny the operation.

The number of men detained in 2017 is given as more than 100 and possibly several hundred, and the December 2018 purge figure of around 40 detained with two killed rests on reporting rather than an official record.

Chechnya's general homicide rate is not in the source inventory, so the deaths documented in the purge cannot be compared against the background rate of violence in the republic, and the counts should not be read as a measured rate.

The April 2017 investigation by Novaya Gazeta into torture and killings of gay men produced no criminal case, and no judicial finding on the 2017 or 2018 events has been identified.
